:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Recall that for $x >0,$ we have 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\ln{x}) = \dfrac 1 x.
$$

We can generalize this to all values $x\neq 0$ by including an absolute value inside the natural logarithm: 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\ln{|x|}) = \dfrac 1 x.
$$

Therefore, the integral of the reciprocal function is

$$
\int \dfrac 1 x \,\textrm{d}x = \ln |x| + C.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $2$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\dfrac 1 x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the integral of $\dfrac 1 {2x} + 3x$ with respect to $x.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{2x}+3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x+\int 3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+3\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}ln⁡|x|+3\cdot \frac{{x}^{1+1}}{1+1}+C \\  & =\frac{ln⁡|x|}{2}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating the Sum of a Reciprocal Function and a Power Function

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C = \ln K,$ where $K>0$ is some other constant. Then, using the laws of logarithms, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}|x|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}|x|+\operatorname{ln}K \\  & =\operatorname{ln}(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+2\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =3 \ln K$ where $K$ is some other constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+C \\  & =3ln⁡|x|+2x+3ln⁡K \\  & =3ln⁡(K|x|)+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms
